questions.text: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
questions.rubric: WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregate functions; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregates (e.g. COUNT(*) > 5). Both can appear in one query; filtering early with WHERE is usually cheaper.

answers.strong: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping or aggregation happens, so it cannot reference aggregate functions. HAVING filters the groups produced by GROUP BY, after aggregation, so it can use conditions like COUNT(*) > 5 or SUM(amount) > 1000. A query can use both: WHERE to drop rows early, which is usually cheaper, and HAVING to filter on the aggregated result.
answers.partial: WHERE filters rows and HAVING is used together with GROUP BY.
answers.subtle: WHERE filters rows before grouping and HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY. HAVING is faster than WHERE because it works on fewer rows, so you should move filters on ordinary columns from WHERE into HAVING.
answers.wrong: WHERE and HAVING are the same thing; HAVING is just the newer syntax for WHERE introduced in SQL:2016, and both can be used interchangeably anywhere.

questions.text: What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python?

answers.strong: Both are ordered sequences that allow duplicates and indexing. A list is mutable: you can append, remove or change items. A tuple is immutable once created. Because of that, a tuple whose elements are all hashable is itself hashable and can be a dictionary key or set member; a list never can. Tuples are a bit lighter and suit fixed records like coordinates, lists suit collections that change.
answers.partial: A list uses square brackets and a tuple uses parentheses. Tuples can't be changed.
answers.subtle: Lists are mutable and tuples are immutable. Because tuples are immutable, any tuple can be used as a dictionary key, even one that contains lists.
answers.wrong: A tuple is a list that keeps itself sorted automatically, and a list can only hold elements of one type.

questions.text: What is idempotency in an ETL pipeline and how do you achieve it?
questions.rubric: A rerun with the same input yields the same final state. Achieved via upserts/MERGE on a business key, partition overwrite, deterministic outputs, dedupe, and tracking processed batches/watermarks.

answers.strong: Idempotency means running the same load several times with the same input leaves the target in the same final state as running it once. I achieve it by upserting with MERGE on the business key instead of blind inserts, overwriting whole partitions for a batch date, and recording processed batch ids or a watermark so a retry skips work that already finished.
answers.partial: It means rerunning the job does not create duplicates. I upsert rows.
answers.subtle: Idempotency means a rerun gives the same final state. I achieve it by appending each run's rows with a load timestamp column, so reruns are safe because every row is unique.
answers.wrong: Idempotency means the pipeline runs faster each time because the data is cached, so you should always append new rows and never worry about duplicates.
answers.idk: I'm not sure, I haven't come across that term.

questions.text: What is overfitting in machine learning and how can you reduce it?

answers.strong: Overfitting is when a model learns noise and quirks of the training data instead of the general pattern, so training error is low but validation or test error is high. You reduce it with more training data, regularisation such as L1/L2 or dropout, a simpler model, early stopping on a validation set, cross-validation to detect it, and data augmentation.
answers.partial: When the model is too good on the training data. Use more data.
answers.subtle: Overfitting is when the model fits noise in the training data, so training error is low but test error is high. The best fix is to add more features and keep training for more epochs until the validation error stops changing.
answers.wrong: Overfitting is when the model is too simple to learn the data, so you fix it by training for many more epochs and adding more features.

questions.text: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?

answers.strong: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: it does a handshake, delivers bytes in order, retransmits lost segments and applies flow and congestion control. UDP is connectionless and sends independent datagrams with no delivery or ordering guarantees and less overhead, so it suits DNS, live streaming and games where low latency matters more than reliability.
answers.partial: TCP is reliable and UDP is faster.
answers.subtle: TCP is connection-oriented with ordered, reliable delivery and retransmission, while UDP is connectionless. UDP still guarantees that packets arrive in order; it just skips the handshake, which is why it is faster.
answers.wrong: UDP is the reliable one because it checks every packet twice, and TCP is used for video games because it has no handshake.

questions.text: What is the difference between a process and a thread?

answers.strong: A process is a running program with its own address space and resources; processes are isolated and talk through IPC. Threads live inside a process and share its memory, heap, globals and open files, but each has its own stack and registers. Threads are cheaper to create and switch between, but shared memory means they need synchronisation, and one thread crashing can bring down the whole process.
answers.partial: A process is a running program and a thread is a part of a process.
answers.subtle: A process has its own memory space and the threads inside it share that memory. Each thread also gets its own private copy of the heap, so threads never need locks for objects on the heap.
answers.wrong: A thread is a bigger unit than a process: one thread contains several processes that all share a single CPU core.
answers.idk: I don't really know the difference.

questions.text: What is a race condition and how do you prevent one?

answers.strong: A race condition is when the result depends on the timing of threads accessing shared state, for example two threads doing read-modify-write on the same counter and losing an update. You prevent it with mutual exclusion such as locks or mutexes, with atomic operations, or by avoiding shared mutable state through immutability or message passing, keeping critical sections small to limit contention and deadlock risk.
answers.partial: It's when two threads use the same variable at once. You can use a lock.
answers.subtle: A race condition is when the outcome depends on the timing of threads accessing shared state. Declaring the shared counter volatile prevents it, because volatile makes count++ an atomic operation.
answers.wrong: A race condition is when one thread runs faster than the others, and you prevent it by raising that thread's priority so it always wins.

questions.text: What is a cache, what is cache invalidation, and what is one strategy for it?
questions.rubric: A cache keeps copies of data in faster storage to reduce latency and load. Invalidation keeps cached data consistent with the source: TTL expiry, cache-aside with delete-on-write, write-through, versioned keys. Trade-off: freshness versus hit rate and load.

answers.strong: A cache keeps a copy of frequently read data in faster storage, such as Redis in front of a database, to cut latency and database load. Invalidation means removing or updating cached entries when the source changes so readers do not get stale data. Strategies include a TTL so entries expire, cache-aside where the application deletes the key on every write and reloads it on the next miss, and write-through where writes update the cache and the database together. The trade-off is freshness against hit rate.
answers.partial: A cache stores data so it is faster to read. Invalidation is clearing it. You can use a TTL.
answers.subtle: A cache keeps copies of hot data in faster storage like Redis, and invalidation removes stale entries. With a TTL the cache can never return stale data, because entries are refreshed the moment the database changes.
answers.wrong: A cache is a backup copy of the database used for disaster recovery, and invalidation means deleting the backup once it gets too old.

questions.text: What does a LEFT JOIN return in SQL?

answers.strong: A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, plus the matching rows from the right table. Where a left row has no match, the right table's columns come back as NULL. Unlike an INNER JOIN, unmatched left rows are kept. A filter on the right table belongs in the ON clause; putting it in WHERE removes the NULL rows and effectively turns it into an inner join.
answers.partial: It returns rows from the left table and some rows from the right.
answers.subtle: A LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus the matches from the right, with NULLs where there is no match. A filter on the right table in the WHERE clause, like WHERE r.status = 'active', still keeps those unmatched left rows.
answers.wrong: A LEFT JOIN returns only the rows that exist in both tables, sorted by the left table's key.

questions.text: What does a Python generator do, and why would you use one?

answers.strong: A generator is a function that uses yield; calling it returns an iterator that produces values lazily, one at a time, keeping its local state between yields. Because it never builds the whole sequence in memory it suits large files, streams and even infinite sequences, and generators compose into pipelines. A generator object can be iterated only once. Generator expressions like (x * x for x in items) are the inline form.
answers.partial: A generator uses yield to return values.
answers.subtle: A generator is a function that uses yield and produces values lazily, which saves memory. You can loop over the same generator object as many times as you like, because it starts again from the beginning each time.
answers.wrong: A generator is a Python tool that generates random numbers, like random.randint, and is mainly used for simulations.
